title: Earthquakes
aka: the earthquake in the days of Uzziah
lead: The land of Israel lies along an active fault, and the Bible remembers its earthquakes. One was so great that people still dated events by it centuries later. Quakes mark God's coming at Sinai and in the psalms. They mark the death and resurrection of Jesus, Paul's release at Philippi, and the judgments of Revelation.

sections.b:
The Jordan valley, the Dead Sea and the Sea of Galilee lie on the Dead Sea Transform. This is the boundary where the African and Arabian plates grind past each other. The Jordan valley part of the fault is thought to have broken in the great earthquake of AD 749, and again in 1033.

The Bible's best-remembered quake dates the book of Amos: "two years before the earthquake" (Amos 1:1; Hebrew ha-ra'ash), in the reign of Uzziah. Centuries later Zechariah still says, "You will run away just as you ran from the earthquake in the time of King Uzziah of Judah" (Zechariah 14:5). At Hazor, Yigal Yadin's digs in the 1950s found tilted and fallen walls and leaning pillars in a layer from the 700s BC (Stratum VI). That layer comes before the Assyrian conquest of 732 BC, and some link its damage with the quake of Amos's day.

Josephus tells a later tradition. When Uzziah went into the temple to burn incense, "a great earthquake shook the ground and a rent was made in the temple." The sun's rays fell on the king's face, and he was struck with skin disease (Antiquities 9.10.4). The account in 2 Chronicles 26:16–21 tells of the incense and the disease, but it says nothing of a quake. Josephus also reports a great earthquake in Judea in Herod's seventh year, when "about ten thousand men also perished by the fall of houses" (Antiquities 15.5.2).

Other shakings in the story: the ground splits and swallows Korah's company (Numbers 16:31–33). During Jonathan's raid "The ground itself quaked. It was a trembling from God" (1 Samuel 14:15).

sections.h: The earth shakes when God comes
sections.b: At Sinai "the whole mountain quaked hard" (Exodus 19:18). The psalms and prophets describe God's coming the same way: "The earth heaved and quaked" (Psalm 18:7; compare Judges 5:4–5; Psalm 68:8; Psalm 104:32; Psalm 114:4; Nahum 1:5; Isaiah 29:6). Ezekiel foresees "a great earthquake" in the land of Israel on the day of Gog (Ezekiel 38:19). Haggai's "I am about to shake the heavens and the earth" is taken up in Hebrews 12:26–27 (see The Shaking of the Heavens and the Earth). Yet when Elijah stood on the mountain, "The LORD was not in the quake." He came after it, in "a sound of thin silence" (1 Kings 19:11–12). For the believer the shaking is no cause for terror: "So we will have no fear when the earth changes place" (Psalm 46:2).

sections.h: In the Gospels, Acts and Revelation
sections.b:
Jesus lists "famines and earthquakes in place after place" among the troubles before the end (Matthew 24:7; Mark 13:8; Luke 21:11). But he adds that "the end is not here yet" (Matthew 24:6). "All these things are only the start of the labor pains" (Matthew 24:8).

Only Matthew tells of the earthquakes at the cross and the tomb. When Jesus died, "The earth quaked and the rocks broke apart," and tombs were opened (Matthew 27:51–54). On Easter morning "the ground shook hard" as the angel rolled the stone away (Matthew 28:2). Readers differ on the opened tombs. Michael Licona suggested that the raised saints may be apocalyptic imagery (The Resurrection of Jesus, 2010). Norman Geisler and Albert Mohler charged that this denied the Bible's inerrancy. The opened graves also call to mind God's promise in Ezekiel, "Look, I am opening your graves" (Ezekiel 37:12), though Matthew does not cite it.

In Acts the place where the believers prayed "shook" (Acts 4:31). At Philippi "a strong earthquake struck" and the prison doors swung open (Acts 16:26).

In Revelation an earthquake comes with the sixth seal (Revelation 6:12). Another follows the seventh seal, just before the trumpets (Revelation 8:5). One strikes during the sixth trumpet (Revelation 11:13), and one at the seventh (Revelation 11:19). The last comes at the seventh bowl, "one with no equal since people came to be on the earth" (Revelation 16:18). How literally to read these visions is discussed under The Tribulation.

common: Every great earthquake is a sign that the end has come; Jesus says of such troubles that "the end is not here yet" (Matthew 24:6).
uncommon: Josephus tells that the earthquake in Uzziah's day split the temple when the king went in to burn incense.
